newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - American's Eagle orders more jets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - American's Eagle orders more jets.

text.p: U.S. airline AMR Corp's domestic carrier American Eagle announced orders on Tuesday for up to 117 short-range passenger jets worth $2.4 billion, splitting the business between rival manufacturers.

At the Paris air show, American reported that it was buying the new 70-seat version of Canadian firm Bombardier's Canadair regional jet but rejected the current 50-seat version in favour of Brazilian rival Embraer's EMB-145 aircraft.

American Eagle's senior vice president, Peter Pappas, told a joint news conference with Embraer that it was buying 42 of its 50-seat regional jets and taking options on a further 25 aircraft. Embraer said the firm order was worth $700 million.
Pappas then joined Bombardier Aerospace management to announce a separate order for 25 Canadair CRJ 700 aircraft worth $700 million, with an option for 25 more aircraft.
The order makes American the launch customer for the 70-seat aircraft, powered by the new CF34-8C engine being developed by General Electric Co and with deliveries due to start in the year 2001.
Bombardier was also short-listed in a "fly-off" earlier this year with Embraer for the 50-seat requirement but made clear it was undercut on price.
"Quite simply the commercial terms on this aircraft were not acceptable to us," Bombardier Aerospace president Robert Brown told reporters.
"We are reorganising ourselves and we feel we are going to be very competitive in the 50-seat category," he added. "We're not going to be in the same position...in the future."
"The competition was fierce but at the end of the day Embraer emerged as our choice," Pappas said. "The EMB-145 is very efficient, capable and we expect profitable."

The twin-engined Embraer aircraft will be powered by AE 3007A1 engines made by Allison Engine Co, the U.S. subsidiary of British aero-engine manufacturer Rolls-Royce Plc. Allison said that the order was worth in excess of $275 million.

Eagle's move into jets follows completion of a radical overhaul of the airline's operations and the recent settlement of a dispute with pilots at AMR's mainline carrier American Airlines over Eagle's plans to start operating jets.
Currently Eagle flies 200 turboprop aircraft on routes covering 127 cities across the U.S., Canada and the Caribbean and connecting into American Airlines' main hubs.
"We have spent the last two years restructuring Eagle to make it a leaner and more competitive regional carrier," Pappas said. "Now Eagle is ready to enter the jet arena..."
Pappas said the new fleet would provide additional capacity and allow the airline to replace some of its turboprop aircraft.

"American Eagle is entering a new phase," he told reporters. "At the present time these aircraft will be growth aircraft but over time we will be replacing some of our turboprops ... depending on demand in the marketplace," he said.
"Eagle is running at big load factors...and customers are demanding regional jets."
